A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same benchmark, renamed from ImplicitQA to VRR-QA, with matching authors, core data, categories and retained experiments. Text, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations, frame and model scaling experiments, reasoning-prompt comparisons, dataset analyses and a human baseline.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds model evaluations, diversity measurements and controlled human evaluations of inferred counting.

M1.justification: The annotation pipeline, category assignment procedure and proposed structured reasoning prompt remain unchanged. The prompt moves from Figure 19 to Figure 20; newly evaluated models and thinking modes are experimental comparisons rather than changes to a proposed method.

E1.justification: The core 1,000-pair movie benchmark and nine reasoning categories remain unchanged. Table 2 extends empirical diversity comparisons to VSI-Bench, Open-EQA and MovieChat, while Appendix F.1 adds expert participants to the human evaluation.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Gemini 3 Flash, Claude 4.5 Sonnet and GPT-5.2, including thinking-enabled variants of the latter two. Table 4 additionally evaluates LongVILA-R1. These substantially expand the evaluated comparator set while retaining the earlier models.

E3.justification: The main 16-frame accuracy and macro-average protocol is retained. Added experiments introduce thinking-enabled configurations, LongVILA-R1 settings spanning 8–128 frames, and counting evaluations controlling expertise and replay access while measuring response time. These extend existing evaluation coverage without establishing changes to earlier runs.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands validation through video-source diversity analysis, counting controls for expertise and replay, and expert annotation-agreement analysis. Thinking-mode comparisons and LongVILA-R1 frame sensitivity add further diagnostic evidence. Earlier prompt, scale, genre, media-type, difficulty and qualitative analyses remain.

E5.justification: Appendix E retains the same five independent Qwen2.5-VL runs and mean/standard-deviation reporting. Appendix F.1 newly quantifies annotation reliability across five experts: 49 of 58 counting questions have unanimous agreement, five have four agreeing, and four have three agreeing.

E6.justification: Substantial new entries include Gemini 3 Flash at 61.8% overall, GPT-5.2 at 50.8% and its thinking-enabled variant at 56.8%, plus the LongVILA-R1 sweep. Table 7 reports replay-enabled counting accuracy of 82.8% for non-experts and 87.3% for experts. Table 2 adds diversity measurements. Existing overall o3 and human scores remain 64.1% and 83.0%.

T1.justification: The hardness-score construction and existing mathematical content are retained. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption or substantive mathematical derivation appears.

C1.justification: v3 narrows the headline contribution to implicit visual relational reasoning. The introduction replaces its claimed performance drop against standard benchmarks with a gap to human performance. The core benchmark contribution, human–model gap and limited benefits from scaling remain.

C2.justification: Appendix F.1 newly attributes weak human counting performance partly to single-viewing restrictions and explains the benefit and time cost of replay. Section 3.2 adds arguments that source diversity matters beyond dataset size and that manual question writing explains greater textual diversity.

D1.justification: Appendix A changes a planned release upon acceptance into a stated public Apache-2.0 release of the benchmark, annotation tools and evaluation resources, with a project URL. v3 also discloses the original human baseline's single-viewing restriction and expert agreement details. Hardware and existing prompt/tool instructions remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds references covering newer models and reasoning research, including IntentQA, ViLMA, STAR and LongVILA-R1. Table 1 adds a dynamic-scene distinction separating movie videos from static-scan benchmarks. The principal positioning against visual-only and audiovisual benchmarks remains intact.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introductory narrative are substantially rewritten around visual relational reasoning, with terminology updated throughout. Diversity becomes a dedicated subsection, the supplementary outline is expanded, and references move from before the appendix to the document's end.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout and extensively rearranges and redraws displays. Existing examples become a front-page teaser and revised Figure 2; the duration plot moves to the supplement. Tables gain rows and columns, Table 7 is added, and the questions-per-video histogram is replaced by an existing genre distribution.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens the paper through newer model comparisons, clearer diversity evidence, and counting controls that explain the earlier low human score while documenting annotation agreement. The reported public release improves reproducibility information. These are useful incremental gains: the central benchmark and principal findings remain stable, and the additional human validation covers only inferred counting.
